items.item: A mean is only a legitimate aggregate over values that live on an interval scale — a machine-state code is nominal, and averaging nominal codes produces a number with no referent at all, not merely an imprecise one.

at.step: Reveal: the wrong aggregate

items.item: LOCF and linear interpolation fail in the same direction for exactly the opposite reason: LOCF assumes nothing changed, interpolation assumes a smooth path — both assumptions are falsified by the same real excursion, which is why neither method is 'safer' in general, only safer for a particular signal's typical behavior.

at.step: Reveal: two fills, one hidden excursion

items.item: A fill flag turns an invisible assumption (this value is real) into a visible one (this value was produced by a rule), which is the same move this chapter already made for event time (topic 7) — writing down which decision was made, rather than leaving it to be inferred from which column happens to be populated.

at.step: Reveal: the max-gap rule and the fill flag

items.item: The max-gap threshold is a policy, not a law of the signal — it should be set from the signal's own expected report period (a sensor that reports every 10 seconds has a very different 'suspiciously long gap' than one that reports every 10 minutes), so a single site-wide default is itself a kind of wrong-aggregate bug one level up.

at.step: Reveal: the max-gap rule and the fill flag

items.item: Declaring a signal's type as tag metadata, rather than inferring it from the data stream, matters because a step signal can look continuous over a short enough window (few transitions) and a slow continuous signal can look like a step signal if sampled too coarsely — inference from shape alone is not reliable at arbitrary window lengths.

at.step: Reveal: a signal needs a declared type before it has an aggregate

items.item: An honest aggregate that reports 'how many of each flag contributed' (not just a number) lets a downstream consumer decide for themselves whether a bucket that's 80% filled is still trustworthy for their purpose — collapsing that to a single number throws away exactly the information a careful reader would need.

at.step: Reveal: the max-gap rule and the fill flag

items.item: A counter's correct aggregate (the difference of end values) is structurally different from the other three types' aggregates (mean, last, max) in that it requires two points, not one, per bucket — which is why a counter resampled the same way as a continuous signal (a mean of raw counter readings) produces a number with no physical meaning at all, a different and worse failure than the state-mean bug.

at.step: Reveal: the right aggregate for each type

items.item: Both fills erasing the same excursion is not a coincidence of this specific dataset — any fill method that only looks at points outside a gap (as both LOCF and linear interpolation do) is mathematically incapable of reconstructing a feature that exists only inside the gap; this is a structural limit of gap-filling, not a tuning problem.

at.step: Reveal: two fills, one hidden excursion

items.item: The same four-hour-outage shape recurs across OT telemetry regardless of plant or vendor, which is why the fill-flag discipline belongs in the resampling layer itself rather than being left to each downstream dashboard to reinvent (and most don't).

at.step: Recap

items.item: A dashboard that never shows a 'missing' region, only ever a continuous line, is not evidence that its sensor never has gaps — it is evidence that someone already chose to fill (and thereby hide) every gap it ever had.
